title: Rain in the Amazon Moves the Centre of the Earth (NASA Measured It)

scenes.text: Rain in the Amazon moves the centre of the Earth.
Every April, the Amazon basin fills with 2,400 billion tons of rainwater.
That weight pulls Earth's centre of mass two millimetres toward South America.
In March, snow across North America and Asia drags it three millimetres toward the North Pole.
NASA tracks the wobble by bouncing lasers off two 900-pound metal disco balls in orbit.
So the whole planet shifts under your feet every time it rains. And NASA can see it.

description:
Rain in the Amazon moves the centre of the Earth.
NASA scientists measured how water, snow and air shifting between the hemispheres pull Earth's centre of mass back and forth by a few millimetres every year, tracked with lasers bounced off the LAGEOS satellites.
What else do you think is heavy enough to move a planet?
first_comment: Bonus: the two laser satellites, LAGEOS 1 and 2, were launched in 1976 and 1992 and are still being tracked from more than 20 countries. What else do you think is heavy enough to nudge a planet?
